title: Predictably Irrational: The Hidden Forces That Shape Our Decisions
author: Dan Ariely
edition_analyzed: Revised and Expanded Edition, if applicable; otherwise, original publication
target_audience: General readers interested in psychology and economics
Students and professionals in behavioral science, economics, and marketing
Individuals curious about decision-making and human behavior
Leaders and policy makers seeking to understand irrational behaviors
core_themes: Influence of context and framing on choices
Social and emotional forces shaping decisions
primary_purpose: To expose the hidden psychological mechanisms and biases that lead people to consistently make irrational choices, undermining the traditional assumption of rational decision-making in classical economics, and to illustrate how understanding these patterns can improve individual decisions and societal outcomes.

structure_format.narrative_style: Engaging, accessible, anecdote-driven with scientific rigor
structure_format.organization: Each chapter focuses on a specific type of bias or irrational behavior, supported by real-life experiments and personal stories
features: Descriptive experiments (most conducted by the author)
Summaries and practical takeaways at chapter ends

key_concepts_lessons: Humans are systematically irrational in predictable ways.
Context, anchoring, and relative comparisons profoundly shape choices.
The price of free—how zero cost distorts value and decision-making.
Ownership and the endowment effect: why we overvalue what we own.
Procrastination, self-control, and the power of immediate gratification.
Social norms and expectations can override economic incentives.
Understanding biases enables us to design better choices and environments.
notable_features: First-hand experimental data explained in easy-to-understand terms
Breaks down complex behavioral economics ideas for non-specialists
Broad real-world applicability, from shopping behavior to public policy
cultural_historical_context: Emerging from the field of behavioral economics, the book was published as public and academic interest was growing in understanding why people deviate from economic rationality. Ariely’s work popularized behavioral economics and contributed toward broader adoption of behavioral insights in business and government.
reception_impact: International bestseller and influential text in behavioral science
Helped popularize the field of behavioral economics for a wide audience
Widely praised for its humor, clarity, and real-world relevance
Cited as foundational in business, economics, and psychology courses
Inspired other books and public policies based on behavioral insights
comparable_titles: Nudge: Improving Decisions about Health, Wealth, and Happiness by Richard H. Thaler and Cass R. Sunstein
Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman
The Art of Thinking Clearly by Rolf Dobelli
Misbehaving: The Making of Behavioral Economics by Richard H. Thaler
